content.title: About
content.content: Pheasant is a wild bird of the Phasianidae family, native to Europe and Asia. Cooked pheasant meat has a dark, slightly sweet flavor, a firmer texture, and a higher protein content compared with chicken.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pheasant was domesticated in ancient Rome and served as a delicacy at banquets.
The dark color of pheasant meat comes from its high myoglobin content.
Unlike chicken, pheasants are usually raised free‑range, influencing taste and texture.
Several breeds exist, including golden, silver, and white pheasants.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Cooked pheasant provides about 24 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with beef or pork, pheasant contains less saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Iron in pheasant meat helps maintain hemoglobin levels and prevents anemia.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B6 and B12 vitamins support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Bird allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to poultry, including pheasant.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: High purine levels can be problematic for people with gout.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Raw or undercooked bird meat may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pheasant is commonly roasted, pan‑fried, or braised. It can be served whole, sliced into steaks, or used in stews. Pair with herbs like rosemary or thyme and a splash of citrus to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh pheasant in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the fridge before cooking.
